lessonTitle: Stable Angina: History, Investigation and Long-Term Management

blocks.text: A 59-year-old retired postmaster has stopped twice on the hill to his allotment this month. He describes a tight band across the middle of his chest that spreads to his jaw, and says it fades about three minutes after he stands still. Nothing about it changes when he presses on his ribs or takes a deep breath. The history alone makes coronary disease the most likely diagnosis, and it also tells us what to do next.

blocks.markdown: **Mechanism.** The myocardium extracts about 70% of the oxygen delivered in the coronary blood, so it cannot meet extra demand by extracting more; it can only increase flow. A fixed atheromatous narrowing (usually 70% or more of the lumen) limits that increase. During exertion, heart rate, contractility and wall tension rise, demand outstrips supply and the myocardium becomes ischaemic. Resting flow is adequate, so the pain settles when exertion stops and demand falls. **Stable angina** is this predictable, exertion-related pattern; ischaemia is reversible and there is no necrosis.

blocks.title: Typical angina (three features)
blocks.text: Angina is characterised by: (1) constricting discomfort in the chest, or in the neck, shoulders, jaw or arms; (2) precipitated by physical exertion; (3) relieved by rest or glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) within about 5 minutes. Three features = typical angina; two = atypical angina; one or none = non-anginal chest pain. This three-feature rule is used in UK guidance to estimate the likelihood of coronary disease.

blocks.caption: Cardiac versus common non-cardiac chest pain, as the history separates them.

blocks.title: Scoring the history
blocks.prompt: A 64-year-old man describes central heavy pressure that comes on when he carries shopping up two flights of stairs, spreads to his left arm, and goes away within 2 minutes of resting. How would you classify the pain?

steps.text: Check feature 1: constricting central discomfort radiating to the arm. Present.
Check feature 2: precipitated by exertion (stairs with shopping). Present.
Check feature 3: relieved by rest within about 5 minutes. Present (2 minutes).
All three features are present, so this is typical angina and the pre-test probability of coronary disease is high, particularly given his age and sex.

blocks.markdown:
**Choosing investigations (o2).** First, take a resting ECG (often normal between attacks) and test for anaemia, thyroid disease, lipids, glucose or HbA1c and renal function, since these influence both symptoms and treatment. Then confirm or exclude coronary disease:

- **CT coronary angiography (CTCA):** first-line anatomical test in current UK guidance for people with typical or atypical angina. It shows plaque and the degree of stenosis.
- **Functional (ischaemia) imaging:** stress perfusion MRI, stress echocardiography or SPECT. Used when CTCA is inconclusive or when coronary disease is already known and the question is whether a lesion causes ischaemia.
- **Invasive coronary angiography:** reserved for people whose non-invasive tests are non-diagnostic or who are being considered for revascularisation, because it carries a small procedural risk.
- **Exercise ECG:** an older functional test; a test is judged adequate only if the patient reaches at least 85% of the age-predicted maximum heart rate. Age-predicted maximum heart rate is approximately 220 minus age in years.

blocks.caption: Rule-of-thumb predicted maximum heart rate (beats per minute).
When to use which test (o2).
rows: First-line for typical or atypical angina
Stress perfusion MRI, stress echo, SPECT
Inconclusive CTCA or known disease, to guide revascularisation

blocks.title: Judging whether a treadmill test was adequate
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old woman stops an exercise test at a heart rate of 118 beats per minute with no ECG change. Was the test adequate to exclude ischaemia?

steps.text: Predicted maximum heart rate = 220 - 70 = 150 beats per minute.
Target for an adequate test is 85% of that value: 0.85 x 150 = 127.5 beats per minute.
She reached 118, which is below 127.5, so the test was submaximal. A negative result cannot reliably exclude coronary disease.

blocks.answer: Not adequate: 118 is below the 127.5 beats per minute target, so the negative test is non-diagnostic.

items: Acute relief: GTN spray or tablet under the tongue. It dilates veins (lowering preload and wall tension) and coronary arteries. Advise sitting down; if pain persists after 5 minutes, repeat once, and call emergency services if pain is still present 5 minutes after the second dose.

Symptom prevention, first line: a beta-blocker (for example bisoprolol) or a calcium channel blocker. Beta-blockers lower heart rate and contractility; use caution in asthma. Rate-limiting calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) are an alternative and should not be combined with a beta-blocker; a dihydropyridine (amlodipine) can be combined.
Add-on or alternatives: long-acting nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil or ranolazine, according to specialist guidance and tolerability.

Prognostic prevention: low-dose aspirin (for example 75 mg daily), a statin (for example atorvastatin, high-intensity for established disease), and an ACE inhibitor if diabetes, hypertension or heart failure coexist.

Risk factors: stop smoking, optimise blood pressure and glucose, lose weight, regular activity, and cardiac rehabilitation advice. Revascularisation (PCI or CABG) is considered for refractory symptoms or high-risk anatomy such as left main stem disease.

blocks.title: Setting a lipid target from non-HDL cholesterol
blocks.prompt: A patient with newly confirmed coronary disease has total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L and HDL cholesterol 1.3 mmol/L. UK guidance aims for at least a 40% fall in non-HDL cholesterol on statin therapy. What non-HDL value would meet that aim?

steps.text: Non-HDL cholesterol = total cholesterol - HDL cholesterol = 6.8 - 1.3 = 5.5 mmol/L.
A 40% reduction leaves 60% of the baseline: 0.60 x 5.5 = 3.3 mmol/L.

blocks.answer: Non-HDL cholesterol of 3.3 mmol/L or below achieves a 40% fall.

blocks.title: New or worsening pain is not stable angina
blocks.text: Stable angina is predictable. Angina at rest, of new onset, or rapidly worsening (crescendo) is an acute coronary syndrome and needs emergency assessment, not an outpatient CTCA request.

points: Typical angina = constricting pain, brought on by exertion, relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes; fewer features lower the likelihood of coronary disease.
Investigation: resting ECG and bloods, then CT coronary angiography first line; functional imaging or invasive angiography when CTCA is inconclusive or revascularisation is planned.
Treat with GTN for attacks, a beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker for prevention, plus aspirin, a statin and risk-factor modification.
Revascularisation is for refractory symptoms or high-risk anatomy, not for every patient with a stenosis.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man has a sharp left-sided chest pain that he can localise with one finger. It is worse on twisting and reproduced by pressing on the costochondral junction. Which description best fits?

distractorRationale.a: Angina is constricting, exertional and not reproducible by palpation.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: sharp, localised, movement-related pain reproduced on palpation is musculoskeletal.
distractorRationale.c: Unstable angina is rest or crescendo ischaemic-type pain, not palpation-reproducible.
distractorRationale.d: Dissection causes abrupt severe tearing pain and is not reproduced by touch.

questions.explanation: Pain reproduced by palpation or movement, and sharply localised, points to the chest wall. Angina is a visceral pain that is diffuse, constricting and not altered by touch.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman describes central chest tightness that comes on when she hurries to catch a bus. It does not go away with rest for about 20 minutes. How is this best classified by the three-feature rule?

options.text: Stable angina, so no further tests

distractorRationale.a: Typical angina needs all three features; relief within about 5 minutes is missing.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: constricting pain and exertional trigger are present (2 of 3), but it is not relieved by rest in 5 minutes.
distractorRationale.c: Non-anginal pain has one or none of the features; here two are present.
distractorRationale.d: Prolonged pain not settling with rest warrants assessment, not dismissal.

questions.explanation: Two of the three features (constricting quality, exertional trigger) are present while rest relief is absent, so this is atypical angina. Pain lasting 20 minutes at rest should also prompt consideration of an acute coronary syndrome.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with typical exertional chest tightness and a normal resting ECG is referred for investigation. Which is the most appropriate first-line test in current UK guidance?

distractorRationale.a: Invasive angiography is reserved for inconclusive non-invasive tests or planned revascularisation.
distractorRationale.b: Troponin is for suspected acute coronary syndrome, not stable exertional symptoms.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: CTCA is the first-line anatomical test for typical or atypical angina.
distractorRationale.d: A chest X-ray does not show coronary disease.

questions.explanation: CT coronary angiography is non-invasive and shows coronary anatomy, so it is first line when angina is suspected. Invasive angiography carries procedural risk and is used when non-invasive imaging is non-diagnostic or intervention is planned.

questions.stem: In a 67-year-old woman with exertional chest pain, CT coronary angiography shows a moderate stenosis in the mid left anterior descending artery and the report calls it inconclusive for functional significance. What is the most appropriate next test?

options.text: Repeat CT coronary angiography in 6 months
Functional imaging for inducible ischaemia, such as stress perfusion MRI or stress echocardiography

questions.correctOptionText: Functional imaging for inducible ischaemia, such as stress perfusion MRI or stress echocardiography

distractorRationale.a: Repeating the same test does not answer the functional question.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: functional imaging tests whether the lesion causes ischaemia and guides revascularisation.
distractorRationale.c: Troponin does not assess stable exertional ischaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Surgery before demonstrating ischaemia or high-risk anatomy is not indicated.

questions.explanation: An anatomical stenosis of uncertain significance needs a functional test to see whether it causes ischaemia. That result decides whether invasive angiography and revascularisation are worthwhile.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with confirmed stable angina also has poorly controlled asthma with recent wheeze and uses a salbutamol inhaler daily. Which is the most suitable first-line anti-anginal drug for symptom prevention?

distractorRationale.a: Beta-blockers can provoke bronchospasm and should be avoided or used with great caution in poorly controlled asthma.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker reduces heart rate and demand without bronchoconstriction.
distractorRationale.c: Aspirin is for prognostic prevention, not an anti-anginal drug (and not at 300 mg long term).
distractorRationale.d: A statin lowers cardiovascular risk but does not prevent angina episodes.

questions.explanation: First-line prevention is either a beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker, chosen by comorbidity. Beta-blockers risk bronchospasm in poorly controlled asthma, so a calcium channel blocker is chosen.

questions.stem: How does sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) relieve an angina attack?

options.text: It dilates veins and coronary arteries, lowering preload and wall tension
It blocks the sinus node funny current

questions.correctOptionText: It dilates veins and coronary arteries, lowering preload and wall tension

distractorRationale.a: Correct: venodilation lowers preload and myocardial wall tension, reducing oxygen demand, and coronary dilation helps supply.
distractorRationale.c: This is the statin effect, not an acute action.

questions.explanation: Nitrates release nitric oxide, relaxing vascular smooth muscle. The main benefit in angina is venodilation, which reduces preload and wall tension and so myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with stable angina has total cholesterol 5.9 mmol/L and HDL cholesterol 1.2 mmol/L. Guidance aims for at least a 40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol on statin therapy. What is the highest non-HDL cholesterol value, in mmol/L, that would meet that aim?
questions.explanation: Non-HDL cholesterol = 5.9 - 1.2 = 4.7 mmol/L. A 40% reduction leaves 60%, so the target is 0.6 x 4.7 = 2.82 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man undergoes an exercise ECG. An adequate test requires at least 85% of the age-predicted maximum heart rate, taking the predicted maximum as 220 minus age. What heart rate, in beats per minute, must he reach?
questions.explanation: Predicted maximum heart rate = 220 - 66 = 154 beats per minute. 85% of this is 0.85 x 154 = 130.9, about 131 beats per minute. A negative result at a lower heart rate cannot exclude ischaemia.

questions.stem: Describe how the history is used to separate typical angina, atypical angina and non-anginal chest pain, and explain how this likelihood assessment shapes the choice of investigation.
markingGuide: Three features: constricting pain (chest, neck, jaw, arms), brought on by exertion, relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes
Three features = typical; two = atypical; one or none = non-anginal
Typical or atypical angina: CT coronary angiography is first line
Functional imaging when CTCA is inconclusive or to test whether a lesion causes ischaemia
Invasive angiography when non-invasive tests are non-diagnostic or revascularisation is being considered
Resting ECG and blood tests are done in everyone; non-anginal pain prompts a search for other causes
questions.explanation: Counting the three features gives a pre-test probability of coronary disease, which determines whether anatomical or functional testing is worth doing. Higher probability justifies direct imaging of the coronary arteries, while low probability redirects attention to alternative diagnoses.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with diabetes and a confirmed stable angina diagnosis asks how his condition will be managed over the next years. Outline the anti-anginal, antiplatelet and risk-factor management and the rationale for each.
markingGuide: GTN for acute relief by venodilation and coronary dilation
Beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker first line to lower heart rate and demand; avoid combining beta-blocker with a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker
Second-line options: long-acting nitrate, ivabradine, nicorandil, ranolazine
Statin for lipid lowering and plaque stabilisation
Smoking cessation, blood pressure and glycaemic control, exercise, weight, cardiac rehabilitation
Revascularisation for refractory symptoms or high-risk anatomy
questions.explanation: Management has two aims: reduce symptoms by balancing myocardial oxygen supply and demand, and reduce future events by treating atherosclerosis and thrombotic risk. Diabetes strengthens the case for tight risk-factor control and ACE inhibition.
